bibliographic.title: A Multilevel Framework for AI Governance
bibliographic.authors: Hyesun Choung, Prabu David, John S. Seberger
bibliographic.venue: The Global and Digital Governance Handbook, Routledge, Taylor & Francis Group
bibliographic.citation_apa: Choung, H., David, P., & Seberger, J. S. (2023). A multilevel framework for AI governance. In The Global and Digital Governance Handbook. Routledge, Taylor & Francis Group.

methodology.method_family: conceptual framework development and synthesis of governance guidelines and trust literature
methodology.study_design: theoretical framework paper without empirical data collection
methodology.sector: cross-sector AI governance spanning government, corporations, and citizens
methodology.technology_context: general AI and machine learning systems; ChatGPT cited as a recent NLP example within broader AI literacy discussion

eligibility.decision_rationale: The paper's primary contribution is a multilevel governance framework for AI involving governments, corporations, and citizens, mediated by trust dimensions. It is highly relevant to AI governance and ethics in regulated contexts, but the provided text does not center conversational systems, LLM operational controls, guardrails, observability, or deployment governance specific to conversational AI in regulated environments. ChatGPT appears only as a brief illustrative example for citizen AI literacy.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Automated triage graded the item as central_candidate, but full-text evidence indicates a broad AI governance framework with only peripheral LLM/conversational references; adjudication should confirm role as foundational context rather than central evidence.

appraisal.notes: Conceptual handbook chapter proposing a multilevel governance model grounded in cited international guidelines and trust theory; no empirical sample or validation study is described in the provided text.

cerqual.explanation: The framework is internally coherent and adequately developed for a conceptual governance contribution, but methodological limitations include absence of empirical testing and limited discussion of enforcement mechanisms. Relevance to the review's conversational-LLM-in-regulated-settings focus is partial because LLM and conversational governance are not the paper's main object of study.

rq_alignment: relevance and acceptance of AI by stakeholders

synthesis.main_claim: Ethical principles for trustworthy AI require a mediating multilevel governance structure involving governments, corporations, and citizens, analyzed through dimensions of trust to translate principles into practice and inform policy.
synthesis.contribution: Offers a multidimensional, multilevel model linking stakeholder governance levels with trust in AI to support trustworthy AI, corporate self-governance, and public policy.
synthesis.limitations: The provided text notes opaque ML black-box behavior, nascent explainability methods, unclear enforcement of international principles on technology firms, and uncertainty about how prior AI literacy efforts remain relevant amid rapid AI change such as ChatGPT.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational contextual evidence for structuring governance analysis across institutional levels and trust dimensions; do not treat as central empirical or operational evidence on conversational LLM governance, guardrails, observability, or regulated deployment controls.
